n: In a second letter, Mormon assures Moroni he is still alive but warns that the news is painful. The letter is a raw window into the last years of the Nephite nation.
Mormon reports a lost battle in which three of his officers — Archeantus, Luram, and Emron — and many of his best men were killed. These names appear nowhere else in scripture.
Mormon fears the Lamanites will destroy the Nephites, who refuse to repent and are constantly stirred by Satan to rage against each other.

f.w: Satan stirreth them up continually to anger

n: Mormon keeps preaching, but nothing works: sharp words make them angry, and gentle words make them harden their hearts. He fears the Spirit has stopped working with them.

f.g: plain, direct, cutting words that call out sin.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord hath ceased striving with them

n: Their anger is so intense they seem unafraid of death. They have lost love for one another and constantly crave blood and revenge — the opposite of the charity Mormon taught.

f.w: they have lost their love, one towards another

n: Mormon’s famous counsel: even when people seem hopeless, keep laboring. We have a work to do while in our mortal bodies, to overcome the adversary and find rest in God’s kingdom.

f.g: the mortal body, pictured as a temporary dwelling made of earth.

f.w: if we should cease to labor, we should be brought under condemnation

n: Mormon relays a report from Amoron: the Lamanites captured men, women, and children at the tower of Sherrizah.
The Lamanites killed the men and then forced the starving women and children to eat their bodies. Mormon records these horrors to show how far a society falls without God.
Yet the Nephites were even worse. At Moriantum they captured Lamanite daughters and robbed them of their chastity and virtue, which Mormon calls most precious of all.
After abusing the women, the Nephites tortured and murdered them and ate their flesh as a show of bravery. Their hearts had become utterly hardened.

f.g: as a sign or proof of courage — showing how twisted their values had become.

n: Mormon cries out but cannot even finish his sentence — the grief interrupts him. He calls them a people “without civilization.”
In a sad aside, Mormon notes that only a few years earlier these same people had been civilized and delightful. Decline can come swiftly.
Mormon starts again, still unable to complete the thought, overwhelmed by a people who delight in abomination.

f.g: something utterly detestable, especially in God’s sight.

n: He finishes the question: how could God possibly hold back his judgment from such a people?

f.g: hold back; stop himself from acting.

n: Mormon’s heart cries woe for his people and asks God to bring judgment and remove their sins from his sight. It is the anguished prayer of a prophet who has run out of options.
Widows and daughters still in Sherrizah were left with nothing: what the Lamanites didn’t take, the Nephite army of Zenephi stole. Many elderly women collapsed and died while searching for food.
Mormon’s own army is weak and cut off from Sherrizah. Those who fled to another Nephite army under Aaron suffered terrible brutality there too.
Mormon laments that his people have no order or mercy. He is only one man and can no longer make them obey his commands.
Both sides are equally brutal, sparing no one, delighting in everything except good. The suffering of women and children is beyond words.

f.w: tongue cannot tell, neither can it be written

n: Mormon stops describing the scene. His people are “past feeling” — so hardened that conscience no longer touches them — and more wicked than the Lamanites.

f.g: spiritually numb; no longer able to feel the promptings of conscience or the Spirit.

n: Mormon cannot even pray for God to bless such a people; it would be like asking God to approve their wickedness.

f.g: commend them to God’s care and favor.

n: But he can commend his son to God. He trusts in Christ for Moroni’s salvation and prays Moroni will live to see the Nephites either return to God or be destroyed.

f.w: except they repent and return unto him

n: If the Nephites perish, it will be like the Jaredites, who destroyed themselves through stubborn hearts and lust for revenge.
Many Nephites have defected to the Lamanites. Mormon asks Moroni to write a little if he survives, and hopes to see him soon to hand over the sacred records.

f.w: I have sacred records that I would deliver up unto thee

n: Some of the most beloved words in the Book of Mormon: Mormon urges Moroni not to be crushed by grief, but to let Christ lift him up and to keep Christ’s suffering, mercy, and the hope of eternal life always in mind.

f.w: the showing his body unto our fathers

f.g: patient endurance; bearing with others’ faults over a long time.

n: Mormon closes with a blessing of grace from the Father and from Christ, who sits at God’s right hand until all things are subject to him.

f.w: until all things shall become subject unto him
sitteth on the right hand of his power
